lesson.title: The Nuclear Pull an Electron Actually Feels
lesson.summary: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge an electron experiences once the shielding of other electrons is subtracted out, and it is the mechanism underneath nearly every periodic trend covered so far.
lesson.body:
An electron in a multi electron atom is not attracted to the full charge of the nucleus. Inner electrons sit between the outer electron and the nucleus and cancel out, or shield, part of that positive charge. Effective nuclear charge, abbreviated Zeff, is the net attractive charge left over after that shielding is accounted for, estimated with the simple relationship Zeff equals Z minus S, where Z is the actual number of protons and S is a shielding constant representing how much charge the other electrons block. This idea connects directly to two more basic building blocks: protons, which set the raw nuclear charge Z, and electrons, whose arrangement determines how effectively that charge is blocked.

A rough first estimate treats every core electron as blocking one full unit of nuclear charge and every electron in the same outer shell as blocking essentially nothing, since electrons at the same distance from the nucleus do not shield each other well. Sodium, with eleven protons and a configuration of 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1, has ten core electrons between its lone valence electron and the nucleus, so a crude estimate gives Zeff around 11 minus 10, or about 1. Slater's rules, a more careful method, account for partial shielding from electrons in the same shell and the shell just inside it, giving a better value for sodium's 3s electron of about 2.2, roughly double the crude estimate but still far below the full nuclear charge of 11.

This more careful accounting explains why effective nuclear charge climbs steadily across a period even though the crude shielding picture might suggest otherwise. Moving from sodium to chlorine across period 3, each added proton is only partially shielded by electrons filling the same 3s and 3p orbitals, since electrons in the same shell shield each other weakly. Using Slater's rules, chlorine's outermost 3p electron experiences an effective nuclear charge of about 6.1, nearly three times sodium's 2.2, even though both elements have the same number of core electrons blocking the inner shells. This steady rise in Zeff across a period is the mechanical cause behind rising ionization energy, rising electronegativity, and shrinking atomic radius.

Down a group, effective nuclear charge tells a subtler story. Each new row adds a full shell of core electrons that shield the valence electron almost as well as the shells before it, so Zeff increases only modestly from one period to the next, comparing lithium's 2s electron at about 1.3 to sodium's 3s electron at about 2.2. What changes far more down a group is the principal quantum number itself: the valence electron occupies a shell farther from the nucleus, so even a similar Zeff produces a weaker pull. That is why atomic radius grows substantially down a group and ionization energy drops, even though the electron is not shielded any more effectively than in the row above.

Effective nuclear charge is best understood as the mechanism, not just another item on the list of trends. Ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, and atomic radius all rise and fall the way they do because the valence electrons feel a systematically stronger or weaker net pull from the nucleus, and that net pull is exactly what Zeff quantifies. Every exception encountered so far, like nitrogen's unusually high ionization energy or fluorine's surprisingly modest electron affinity, ultimately traces back to how effectively electrons in a subshell shield or repel one another, refining the simple Zeff equals Z minus S picture into something that matches real measured data.
